Directions for questions 1 to 6: Answer the questions on the basis of the information given below.


A retail store sells five items — laptops, smartphones, headphones, tablets, and smartwatches. Each item is strategically priced by
marking it above the cost price and then offering discounts to attract customers. A profit is earned when the selling price exceeds the cost
price, while a loss occurs when heavy discounts reduce the selling price below the cost price. High-demand items, such as smartphones,
often provide better profit margins, whereas accessories may be discounted more aggressively. By balancing discounts and profit
margins, the store aims to maximize overall profit while remaining competitive. Careful pricing ensures sustainability, customer
satisfaction, and steady revenue growth in a competitive market.


The laptop has a marked price of Rs. 65,000, and after offering a discount of 20%, the shopkeeper earns a profit of Rs. 2,000. The cost
price of the smartwatch is half the cost price of the tablet, and after selling the smartwatch at a discount of 40% on the marked price, the
shopkeeper incurs a loss of 10%. The tablet is sold for Rs. 23,800 after a discount of 15% on the marked price, and the shopkeeper earns a
profit of 19%. The cost price of the smartphone is equal to the sum of the cost prices of the tablet and the smartwatch. The shopkeeper
marks the smartphone at 40% above its cost price, and after offering a discount on the marked price, he earns a profit of 5%. The
headphone is marked 50% above the cost price, and by selling it for Rs. 4,200, the shopkeeper earns a profit of 5%.

Q 1. What percentage above the cost price has the laptop been marked up?

a) 15%

b) 20%

c) 25%

d) 30%


Q 2. What is the marked price of the tablet?

a) Rs.28,400

b) Rs.27,300

c) Rs.28,000

d) Rs.28,700


Q 3. What is the selling price of the smartphone?

a) Rs.32,500

b) Rs.31,500

c) Rs.31,000

d) Rs.30,800


Q 4. What is the combined profit or loss incurred by selling a combination of a smartwatch and headphone?

a) Profit of 6.67%

b) Loss of 3.33%

c) Profit of 4.5%

d) Loss of 5.7%

Q 5. Find the overall profit (in Rs.) of the shopkeeper while selling one unit of each of the five items.

a) 6500

b) 6600

c) 6400

d) 6700


Q 6. During Christmas, the store offers an extra 2.5% discount on the selling price of a laptop. What is the profit or loss incurred (in Rs.)?

a) 560

b) 850

c) 700

d) 660


Directions for questions 7 to 12: Answer the questions on the basis of the information given below.


A newly constructed training institute is planning interior renovation work for selected sections of the building. The renovation includes
flooring work using either granite or laminated wood. All rooms and halls are rectangular in shape. The areas selected for renovation are
as follows:
Reception hall measuring 35 m × 25 m;
Director’s office measuring 15 m × 12 m;
Cafeteria measuring 20 m × 15 m;
Data storage and IT room measuring 22 m × 10 m;
Conference room measuring 33 m × 25 m;


The total area of the institute building is 3000 sq. m. The cost of laminated wooden flooring is Rs.150 per sq. m, while the cost of granite
flooring is Rs.200 per sq. m. The Conference room, Data storage and IT room, and Cafeteria are to be floored with granite. The Director’s
office and Reception hall are to be floored with laminated wood. No other part of the institute requires flooring renovation.

Q 7. What is the cost of flooring for the Data Storage and IT Room?

a) Rs.33,000

b) Rs.42,000

c) Rs.44,000

d) Rs.45,500


Q 8. What is the ratio of the flooring cost of the Reception hall to that of the Conference room?

a) 35 : 33

b) 140 : 99

c) 47 : 33

d) 35 : 44


Q 9. If the four walls and ceiling of the Director’s office (height = 11 m) are to be painted at the rate of Rs.120 per sq. m, what will be the
total renovation cost of the Director’s office including flooring?

a) Rs.92,880

b) Rs.1,19,880

c) Rs.1,17,640

d) Rs.1,21, 840


Q 10. What percentage of the total institute area has been renovated in terms of flooring?

a) 70%

b) 75%

c) 85%

d) 80%


Q 11. What is the total area floored with granite?

a) 1345 sq. m

b) 1335 sq. m

c) 1325 sq. m

d) 1295 sq. m


Q 12. If the remaining area of the institute is to be carpeted at the rate of Rs. 95 per sq. m, how much additional expenditure will be
incurred?

a) Rs.55,000

b) Rs.56,000

c) Rs.58,000

d) Rs.57,000


Directions for questions 13 to 42: Read the passages given below and answer the questions that follow.


Passage – 1


Constitutional democracies do not merely protect the right to speak; they create conditions under which disagreement can survive. Liberty
of thought and expression is valuable not only because it protects individual autonomy but because it enables competing visions of
society to coexist. Fraternity, one of the values recognised in the constitutional framework, requires citizens to acknowledge one another
as equal participants despite differences in belief, ideology, faith, or social identity. It therefore accommodates disagreement and
discourages enforced conformity.


Throughout history, free speech has often enabled individuals and groups lacking social or political power to participate in democratic
discourse. Reform movements seeking equality, dignity, and inclusion have frequently depended upon speech and expression to challenge
existing structures. Therefore, dissenting opinions cannot ordinarily be suppressed merely because they disturb dominant opinion or
unsettle prevailing social norms.


However, constitutional protection of speech does not imply complete immunity. Freedom of expression may be subject to restrictions
where expression threatens constitutionally recognised interests such as public order, decency, morality, security of the State, or the
dignity of particular communities. Yet restrictions imposed upon speech must satisfy the principle of proportionality. The mere existence
of disagreement or discomfort does not justify broad restrictions. Measures adopted must bear a rational connection with the objective
sought and should interfere with speech only to the extent necessary. Constitutional values also distinguish between constitutional

morality and popular morality. Popular morality may reflect majoritarian beliefs, customs, or social attitudes prevailing at a given time.
Constitutional morality, however, derives from principles of equality, dignity, liberty, and justice embedded within the constitutional order.
Constitutional rights cannot ordinarily be denied merely because a majority of people disagree with a particular belief or expression.


Furthermore, threats to free expression may arise not only through direct governmental action but also through organised private conduct.
If private groups use intimidation, social pressure, economic retaliation, or coordinated harassment to silence unpopular views, the
practical value of free speech may become illusory. In such circumstances, the State may possess a positive obligation not merely to
avoid suppressing expression itself, but also to ensure that individuals are not effectively prevented from exercising their constitutional
freedoms. Finally, constitutional values are often best assessed from the standpoint of those who remain vulnerable or excluded from
dominant structures. Justice and equality cannot be evaluated merely through the experiences of those who already possess social or
economic privilege. Constitutionalism frequently requires attention to the perspectives of those whose voices remain unheard.

Q 13. A student group organises a peaceful event criticising a recently enacted policy. University authorities prohibit the gathering
because several influential alumni state that the event may damage the institution’s image and create discomfort among certain
sections of society. No evidence suggests violence or disruption. Which option most appropriately applies the passage?

a) The prohibition appears justified because institutional reputation outweighs expressive freedoms.

b) The prohibition appears unjustified because disagreement alone cannot ordinarily justify suppression of expression.

c) The prohibition is justified because discomfort among influential groups amounts to a threat to public order.

d) The prohibition becomes justified if the majority of students oppose the event.


Q 14. A State government prohibits all online discussion regarding a controversial urban redevelopment project after discovering that a
few individuals had posted threatening messages concerning the project. The order bans every discussion, including academic debate
and criticism. Which option best follows?

a) The order appears disproportionate because restrictions must not exceed what is necessary to achieve a legitimate objective.

b) The order is justified because some unlawful speech permits complete suppression of related discussions.

c) The order is justified because administrative convenience outweighs expressive interests.

d) The order is constitutional because public projects cannot be criticised during implementation.


Q 15. A municipal authority refuses permission for a cultural exhibition because surveys indicate that a majority of residents consider
its themes morally inappropriate. No evidence suggests threats to security, public order, or community dignity. Which option best applies
the passage?

a) Permission should be denied because majoritarian moral beliefs determine constitutional rights.

b) Permission should be denied because public disagreement automatically creates constitutional restrictions.

c) Permission should ordinarily be granted because constitutional morality cannot be replaced by majoritarian opinion.

d) Permission should be denied because cultural expression receives weaker protection than political speech.


Q 16. An independent journalist publishes investigative reports exposing corruption. While the government takes no action against him,
several private organisations pressure advertisers to terminate contracts, publicly reveal his personal information, and threaten
institutions hosting his lectures. Which option most appropriately follows?

a) No constitutional issue exists because only State action affects freedom of speech.

b) Constitutional concerns arise because private coercive conduct may substantially undermine free expression.

c) The conduct remains permissible because economic pressure forms part of ordinary public debate.

d) Constitutional concerns arise only if criminal proceedings are initiated.

Q 17. A film repeatedly portrays members of a particular linguistic community as dishonest and socially inferior through recurring
stereotypes and imagery. The producers argue that artistic freedom protects all forms of representation. Which option best applies the
passage?

a) The expression may attract constitutional concern because constitutional values protect community dignity.

b) The expression should automatically remain protected because fictional works cannot create constitutional harm.

c) The expression becomes objectionable only if violence occurs after release.

d) The expression should remain protected because artistic freedom overrides all competing interests.


Q 18. A scholarship policy allocates educational resources solely based on existing performance rankings without considering whether
historically disadvantaged groups face structural barriers affecting their opportunities. Which approach most closely follows the
passage?

a) The policy should be examined primarily from the perspective of individuals already benefiting from existing structures.

b) The policy should be assessed only by examining average economic outcomes.

c) The policy should be evaluated from the standpoint of individuals whose voices or interests remain marginalised.

d) The policy should automatically be upheld because identical treatment always guarantees equality.


Directions for questions 13 to 42: Read the passages given below and answer the questions that follow.


Passage – 2


Negligence originates from the Latin term “negligentia,” meaning “failure to pick up” or “neglect.” At its core, negligence refers to
carelessness or a failure to exercise the degree of care that a reasonable person would, resulting in harm to another. To establish
negligence, several essential elements must be proved. First, there must be a duty of care, meaning the defendant must owe a legal
obligation to act with reasonable caution toward the plaintiff. This duty arises when one person’s actions may reasonably and foreseeably
affect another’s safety, and its existence depends on the relationship between the parties. Secondly, there must be a breach of duty, which
occurs when the defendant fails to act as a reasonable person would under similar circumstances. The standard of care is assessed
objectively by comparing the defendant’s conduct to that of an ordinarily prudent person.


Another requirement is causation, meaning the breach of duty must directly result in harm to the plaintiff. Causation consists of two
components. The first is actual or factual causation, commonly assessed using the “but for” test, which asks whether the harm would
have occurred but for the defendant’s act. The second is legal or proximate causation, which examines whether the harm was a
reasonably foreseeable consequence of the defendant’s actions. Further, the plaintiff must establish damage, demonstrating that actual
injury or loss resulted from the defendant’s negligence. Foreseeability also plays an important role in negligence law, as the harm suffered
must have been reasonably foreseeable at the time of the negligent act. A person generally cannot be held liable for highly unusual or
remote consequences that could not reasonably have been anticipated.


The law also adopts an objective standard through the reasonable person standard, which asks how an ordinarily prudent individual would
have acted in the same situation. Personal limitations or characteristics of the defendant, such as carelessness or inexperience, are
generally not considered relevant in determining liability.


Certain defenses may also be available in negligence actions. One such defense is contributory negligence, which arises when the plaintiff
contributes to his or her own harm by failing to take reasonable care for personal safety. In such situations, although the defendant may
have acted negligently, the plaintiff’s own negligence may reduce or completely bar recovery of damages. Another defense is an Act of
God (Vis Major), which refers to extraordinary natural events beyond human control or foresight that cannot be prevented despite
reasonable care. Since such events are unforeseeable and irresistible, the defendant is generally not held liable if the harm resulted solely
from them.

Closely related is the concept of an inevitable accident, which refers to an event that could not have been prevented despite the exercise of
reasonable care, caution, and skill. Unlike an Act of God, an inevitable accident may arise from human conduct rather than natural forces.
Finally, the doctrine of Res Ipsa Loquitur, meaning “the thing speaks for itself,” serves as a rule of evidence in negligence cases. It applies
where the precise cause of an accident may be unknown, but the nature of the incident itself strongly suggests that it could not ordinarily
have occurred without negligence.


Source: https://www.manupatracademy.com

Q 19. D, a surgeon performed invasive surgery for appendix removal. The patient’s family wanted laser surgery instead, as it would heal
earlier. D was of the opinion that the patient’s case is critical, therefore it would be in the best interest to perform invasive surgery. During
the procedure which was conducted with due care and caution, the patient inadvertently developed an infection, which shifted to the
intestines. The family blamed the doctor for negligence. Decide whether doctor could be held liable?

a) The doctor is not liable, because he was not negligent, he just chose an alternative medical procedure.

b) The doctor is not liable, because he was not aware of the potential consequence of invasive surgery.

c) The doctor is liable because he chose a procedure which amplified the complications.

d) The doctor is liable because he is responsible for the patient’s infection.


Q 20. Two friends, T and R went in a shop. The skylight of the shop was broken and not repaired. A portion of the glass fell and hit T,
causing him injuries on the head. R, when saw the glass falling on T, clutched his arm to pull him aside, in the process, R injured his hand,
and amplified the injury in his already fractured wrist. Decide whether R can claim compensation for negligence?

a) R cannot claim compensation for negligence because he knew the risk and danger of helping T.

b) R can claim compensation for negligence only for the actions that were consequent to the negligence of the shop.

c) R cannot claim compensation because the glass fell on T.

d) R can claim compensation because he also sustained severe injury.


Q 21. G, a shipowner was carrying R’s zebra as a carrier by sea. During a turbulent stormy weather, the zebra turned hostile and behaved
violently leading to injuries, despite the best efforts from the crew. Decide whether G could be held liable for negligence?

a) G can be held liable for negligence because he is the owner of the ship.

b) G can be held liable for negligence because R entrusted G with the duty to care.

c) G cannot be held liable for negligence because this was an act of god.

d) G cannot be held liable for negligence because he was not part of the crew.


Q 22. J a scientist was researching about the cure of foot and mouth disease in the cattle. He conducted experiments on several cows.
However, the virus escaped and infected some cattle in the neighbourhood. The infected cattle had to be culled to prevent the infection
from spreading further. The owners of the cattle were compensated. Meanwhile a few days later, a cattle auction was scheduled to take
place. The cattle auctioneers demanded compensation as well. Decide whether J could be held liable for his negligence towards the
cattle auctioneer?

a) J could be held liable for negligence as the loss to the auctioneers was foreseeable.

b) J could be held liable for negligence because auctioneers suffered economic loss.

c) J could not be held liable for negligence because it pertains to loss of profits.

d) J could not be held liable for negligence because the loss of the auctioneers was not foreseeable.

Q 23. Which of the following situation does not describe a valid defence against negligence?

a) The patient voluntarily accepted the risk involved in emergency treatment.

b) The harm was partly due to the patient’s own failure to disclose allergy history.

c) The act was done in good faith with the intention to save life.

d) The situation was an inevitable accident beyond reasonable human control


Q 24. Which of the following is not an essential element to establish liability for negligence?

a) Existence of a legal duty to take care

b) Breach of that duty by failure to act as a reasonable person

c) Actual damage suffered by the plaintiff

d) Existence of a wrongful intention to cause harm


Directions for questions 13 to 42: Read the passages given below and answer the questions that follow.


Passage – 3


Whoever intentionally puts any person in fear of any injury to that person, or to any other, and thereby dishonestly induces the person so
put in fear to deliver to any person property or valuable security, or anything signed or sealed which may be converted into a valuable
security, commits “extortion.” Its aim, akin to blackmail, involves dishonestly obtaining payments or benefits from someone by instilling
fear through threats. It occupies a middle ground between theft and robbery. The key components of extortion include intentionally
inducing fear in a person and dishonestly persuading them, under that fear, to surrender property or valuable assets to another individual.


A person must be put in fear of injury. To qualify as fear under extortion, it must be of such intensity as to disrupt the person’s mental
composure and deprive them of free consent. In extortion cases, the validity of the accusation is irrelevant; the mere threat of harm,
whether physical or reputational, constitutes an offence. The term “injury” encompasses harm to body, mind, reputation, or property.


Dishonest inducement is another crucial aspect of extortion and lies in the dishonest inducement. Mere causing of wrongful loss is
insufficient; there must be an intention on the part of the individual instilling fear to cause wrongful loss or gain. The delivery of property or
valuable security by the person put in fear to another person is also essential. For extortion to occur, there must be documented threat or
fear of injury compelling the victim to surrender property to the perpetrator. This fear-induced surrender is essential for the offence.


Criminal activities like extortion and robbery are often misunderstood due to their overlapping elements. However, these crimes are
distinct in their methods, impacts, and legal consequences. Extortion relies on threats and psychological manipulation to unlawfully obtain
money or property, while robbery involves direct force or intimidation, often in the victim’s immediate presence. Robbery involves the direct
and unlawful taking of someone’s property by using force or intimidation. Unlike extortion, robbery typically occurs in the presence of the
victim and involves immediate threats or acts of physical violence.


Source: https://www.defactojudiciary.in

Q 25. G, a member of the legislative assembly, promised the sugar co-operatives that all the pending cases against such co-operatives
would be dismissed if they donated money for the upcoming by-polls in the state. The co-operatives agreed, and donated money. The
election results were not favourable. G however did not dismiss any case against the co-operatives. A case of extortion was filed against
G. Decide.

a) This is not a case of extortion as there was no fear or threat of injury.

b) This is not a case of extortion as the election results were not favourable.

c) This is a case of extortion, as G did not fulfil his promise.

d) This is a case of extortion, as it was a dishonest inducement.

Q 26. V was the nephew of K. They were ensued in a legal battle for the title of a property. V believing that he is the real owner of the
property, tried to remove K from the competition. V even threatened K to kill him, if he does not back down with his demands. One day,
while K was sleeping, V tiptoed into his house and shot him. Next day, V got the papers of the land, from the court. Decide strictly on the
principle mentioned in the passage, whether V could be held liable for extortion?

a) V is not liable for extortion because V got the papers of the land from the court.

b) V is not liable for extortion because there was no dishonest inducement.

c) V is liable for extortion because he threatened K to kill him.

d) V is liable for extortion because he killed K to get the ownership of the land.


Q 27. L was a renowned godman in the region. He received tons of gold and other valuable kinds in donation. M, a person who lived in
the same region, was an ardent follower of L. One day he came to know about L’s secret drug dealing activities. M threatened L to share
with him half of the donations, otherwise he would expose his indiscretions. Decide whether this would amount to extortion?

a) This not a case of extortion because L was indeed involved in drug trafficking.

b) This is a case of extortion by L, as he fools his followers into believing him as a godman.

c) This is a case of extortion because M threatened L for dishonest inducement.

d) This is not a case of extortion because sharing of donations would not amount to dishonest inducement.


Q 28. A, a moneylender, had been demanding repayment of his money from B for several weeks. One evening, A forcibly stopped B on a
deserted road, caught hold of his collar, and pointed a knife at his chest saying, “Give me Rs. 50,000 right now, or I will stab you.” Terrified,
B called his friend C on the phone and asked him to immediately bring Rs. 50,000 to the spot. Within minutes, C arrived and handed over
the money to A in B’s presence, after which A fled. From the options below choose the correct answer.

a) This is extortion because there is an element of dishonest inducement.

b) This is robbery because there was immediate transfer of valuable under threat.

c) This is extortion because there was threat and fear.

d) This is robbery because there was a threat of killing.


Q 29. Under the Indian Penal Code, which of the following is not an essential condition of extortion?

a) Putting a person in fear of injury

b) Dishonest inducement to deliver property

c) Delivery of property as a result of such inducement

d) Fear of instant death or instant hurt


Q 30. Which of the following options best describes the difference between robbery and extortion under the Indian Penal Code?

a) In extortion, property is taken without consent, whereas in robbery, it is taken with consent.

b) In robbery, there is fear of instant harm and immediate delivery of property, whereas in extortion, such immediacy may be absent.

c) Extortion always involves violence, whereas robbery may not involve violence.

d) Robbery requires entrustment of property, whereas extortion does not.

Directions for questions 13 to 42: Read the passages given below and answer the questions that follow.


Passage – 4


A seller is deemed to be an unpaid seller under certain conditions. Firstly, a seller is considered unpaid if the whole price of the goods sold
has not been paid or tendered. Secondly, a seller may also be regarded as unpaid where a bill of exchange or any other negotiable
instrument has been accepted as conditional payment, but the condition remains unfulfilled due to dishonour of the instrument or
otherwise. An unpaid seller possesses certain rights against the goods sold.


One such right is the Right of Lien. The right of lien permits an unpaid seller to retain possession of the goods until payment is made. This
right may be exercised where the goods are sold without any credit terms, where the credit period has expired, or where the buyer
becomes insolvent. Lien is regarded as a “particular lien,” meaning it can be exercised only by the seller and not by any assignee or
creditor. The seller may exercise this right even if the goods are held as an agent or bailee of the buyer. Another important right is the Right
of Stoppage in Transit. This right enables the unpaid seller to stop the goods from being delivered to the buyer and to regain possession
while the goods are still in transit. However, this right becomes available only when the buyer becomes insolvent after the sale. Goods are
regarded as being in transit from the time they are delivered to a carrier until the buyer or the buyer’s agent takes delivery.


The unpaid seller also enjoys the Right of Resale. Where the goods are perishable in nature, the seller may resell them without providing
notice to the buyer. However, where the goods are non-perishable, the seller must provide notice to the buyer and allow a reasonable
period for payment before reselling them. Further, the seller may also resell where an express right of resale has been reserved in the
contract itself. If the seller resells the goods without giving the required notice, the seller cannot recover damages from the buyer for
losses suffered due to the resale. However, where proper notice has been given, the seller may claim damages and also retain any profit
arising from the resale. It is important to distinguish between the right of lien and the right of stoppage in transit. The right of lien remains
available only so long as the unpaid seller continues to retain possession of the goods. In contrast, the right of stoppage in transit arises
only after the seller has parted with possession of the goods, while they are still in the course of transit.


Source: https://www.defactolaw.in/post

Q 31. B sold shares of the company to W. B also delivered the share certificates along with transfer deed. To pay for the shares, W
issued a cheque to B. When B went to encash, the cheque bounced. B decided to exercise his right to lien. As per the passage, choose
the correct option.

a) B cannot exercise his right to lien as he has already transferred the possession of shares.

b) B cannot exerciser his right to lien as shares are movable objects.

c) B can exercise his right to lien as W has not satisfied the payment against the buying of shares.

d) B can exercise his right to lien as a compensation for the bouncing of cheque.


Q 32. R and T entered into a contract whereby R agreed to sell metallic rods to T for a specified price. T paid the entire purchase price in
advance before dispatch of the goods. While the goods were being transported to T’s factory, T inspected the shipment upon arrival and
found that the rods were of inferior quality and therefore rejected the order. Decide whether R has the right of stoppage in transit.

a) R does not have the right to stoppage in transit because the goods were not of the stipulated quality.

b) R does not have the right to stoppage in transit because he has already been paid in full.

c) R does have the right to stoppage in transit because T refused to accept the delivery.

d) R does have the right to stoppage in transit because it is a right available to every seller


Q 33. Y contracted with Z to sell 50 kg of grain on a stipulated day and destination. Z paid 30% of the total price before the delivery and
promised to pay the reminder after the reminder. Meanwhile Y heard that Z has contracted someone else for the same consignment,
therefore Y delivered only 50% of the grain to Z, and asked to him to pay in full, to get the rest 50%. Z did not reply to Y’s proposal. Decide
whether Y could exercise right to lien in this case.

a) Y cannot exercise this right because he was already paid half of the amount.

b) Y cannot exercise this right because he already parted with 50% of the grains.

c) Y can exercise this right on the reminder 50% of the grains.

d) Y can exercise this right on the grain he has delivered to Z.


Q 34. R entered into a contract with S to sell 100 bags of rice. S failed to pay the price on the agreed date. R, after giving due notice to S,
resold the goods to T at a lower price due to a fall in market value. Later, R sued S for the loss incurred on resale. Decide whether R is
entitled to recover the loss.

a) R cannot recover the loss because once goods are resold, the original contract comes to an end.

b) R can recover the loss because he exercised his right of resale after giving notice to S.

c) R cannot recover the loss because resale is only allowed when goods are perishable.

d) R can recover the loss only if S expressly agreed to such resale at the time of contract.


Q 35. Which of the following correctly distinguishes between the right of lien and the right of stoppage in transit under the Sale of
Goods Act?

a)
Right of lien can be exercised even after the seller has parted with possession, whereas stoppage in transit requires possession with the
seller.

b) Right of lien is available only when the buyer becomes insolvent, whereas stoppage in transit is available in all cases of non-payment.

c)
Right of lien is exercised while the seller retains possession of goods, whereas stoppage in transit is exercised after the seller has parted
with possession but the goods are still in transit.

d) There is no substantial difference between the two rights as both arise only after delivery of goods to the buyer.


Q 36. Which of the following options, best describe an unpaid seller?

a) E, a seller received half payment in cash and half in kind.

b) F, a seller, received bill of exchange, which was honoured within the stipulated period.

c) G, a seller received half payment as cash and for other half a promise to pay was made.

d) H, a seller received a promissory note against the goods sold, which was later paid.


Directions for questions 13 to 42: Read the passages given below and answer the questions that follow.


Passage – 5


Contracts are founded upon the principle that parties who voluntarily enter into legally enforceable agreements are expected to perform
the obligations they have undertaken. Ordinarily, a mere increase in difficulty, inconvenience, expense, or hardship does not excuse a party
from performance. However, the law recognises certain situations in which performance may become impossible or fundamentally
different from what the parties originally contemplated. This principle is generally referred to as the doctrine of frustration.


Frustration arises when, after the formation of a valid contract and without fault of either party, an unforeseen event occurs that renders
performance impossible, unlawful, or radically different from what the parties intended at the time of contracting. Such events may include
destruction of the subject matter, change in law, death or incapacity in contracts requiring personal skill, or cancellation of an event that

forms the foundation of the agreement. However, frustration cannot be invoked where the event was foreseeable, where the parties
themselves created the impossibility, or where performance merely became more expensive, less profitable, or commercially inconvenient.


When frustration occurs, the contract is automatically discharged and parties are released from future obligations. However, obligations
already performed prior to frustration may continue to have legal consequences.


Distinct from frustration is breach of contract, which occurs when a party fails to perform a contractual obligation without lawful excuse.
Breach may be actual or anticipatory. An actual breach occurs where a party refuses or fails to perform when performance becomes due.
For example, if a supplier fails to deliver goods on the agreed date, the breach occurs on that date itself.


An anticipatory breach occurs when, before the time fixed for performance arrives, one party either expressly communicates an intention
not to perform the contract or acts in a manner making performance impossible. Upon anticipatory breach, the innocent party generally
has two options. First, the innocent party may immediately treat the contract as terminated and sue for damages. Second, the innocent
party may elect to keep the contract alive and wait until the date of performance. However, if the innocent party chooses to keep the
contract alive and a frustrating event occurs before the performance date, the contract may subsequently be discharged by frustration,
potentially affecting the right to damages.


The law also distinguishes between self-induced impossibility and genuine frustration. A party cannot deliberately create circumstances
preventing performance and later rely upon frustration to escape liability. Thus, if impossibility results from a party’s own actions, the
matter is treated as breach rather than frustration.

Q 37. P entered into a contract with Q to transport luxury furniture to another city for Rs. 10 lakh. Before performance began, fuel prices
increased sharply and transportation costs nearly doubled. P refused to perform, arguing that the contract had become commercially
burdensome and economically impractical. Which of the following is most appropriate?

a) The contract is frustrated because increased expense automatically creates impossibility.

b) P is discharged because commercial hardship and reduced profitability excuse performance.

c) P has committed breach because increased cost alone does not amount to frustration.

d) P is discharged because contracts become void whenever circumstances change significantly.


Q 38. R contracted with S, a famous singer, for an exclusive live performance at a festival. Before the scheduled performance, S
suffered a severe medical condition permanently affecting her ability to sing. Which option best applies?

a) The contract is frustrated because incapacity in a personal service contract destroys the basis of performance.
